howToUse: This is Bonus #3 from your programme: a ready-to-use script bank of seventeen self-coaching prompts you pull out the moment a fear-thought about your writing ability surfaces. Keep this open in a tab whenever you sit down to write copy. Read the script that matches your exact stuck moment, say it out loud or type it back to yourself, then return to the document. It achieves one thing: it stops the fear spiral before it costs you another hour of avoidance.
promise: Use these scripts to redirect "my brain doesn't write" the moment it appears — so you stay in your document and keep moving. Every script is drawn from the same psychology that already makes you brilliant on a discovery call, because that is the same skill set doing the work here.

tools.name: The 17-Script Reframe Bank (By Stuck Moment)
tools.instructions: Find the column that matches your exact stuck moment, pick the script that lands, read it aloud or type it back to yourself, then return to your document.
tools.content:
# The 17-Script Reframe Bank

---

## STUCK MOMENT 1: The Blank Page
*You've opened a new document. The cursor is blinking. Nothing is coming.*

**Script 1**
"I am not trying to write copy right now. I am trying to remember what my client said the week before they booked a call with me. I just need to write that down."

**Script 2**
"My brain doesn't write from nothing — it writes from a conversation. So before I type a single word of copy, I'm going to write two sentences about the last client who said 'you completely get me.' What were they describing when they said it?"

**Script 3**
"Blank pages feel like a test I haven't studied for. They're not. They're just the before-picture. I've seen a lot of before-pictures with clients. I know what to do with a before-picture."

**Script 4**
"The first sentence doesn't have to be good. It has to be true. What is one true thing I know about the person I'm writing this for right now?"

**Script 5**
"I've started a lot of discovery calls with nothing but a name and a booking confirmation. This is that. I know how to get into a conversation from cold."

---

## STUCK MOMENT 2: The Rewrite Loop
*You've rewritten the same sentence eight, ten, twelve times. It still sounds wrong. You're now questioning whether you have anything useful to say.*

**Script 6**
"I am not stuck because I can't write. I am stuck because I'm editing before I've actually finished saying what I mean. What am I actually trying to say here, in one sentence, if I were explaining it to a client on a call?"

**Script 7**
"The version I keep deleting is not wrong — it's just not dressed yet. I'm going to stop rewriting the sentence and write what I mean underneath it in plain language, then come back."

**Script 8**
"When a client is circling the same point on a call and can't land it, I don't tell them to try harder. I ask them a different question. The different question here is: what am I afraid this sentence will reveal if I leave it as it is?"

**Script 9**
"Twelve rewrites means I care about this. Caring about it is not the same as being bad at it. I'm going to pick the version that is most honest and keep moving. I can come back."

**Script 10**
"There is no version of this sentence that every reader will love. There is a version that my specific reader will recognise themselves in. I'm going to write for that one person and stop trying to write for everyone."

---

## STUCK MOMENT 3: The Post-Publish Spiral
*You've hit send or gone live. Now every word looks wrong. You're convinced you've embarrassed yourself and that the silence in your inbox confirms it.*

**Script 11**
"The discomfort I feel right now is not evidence that the copy was bad. It is evidence that I published something real. Those are not the same thing."

**Script 12**
"My clients don't book after reading one email. They book after reading something that made them feel seen — once, twice, over time. This piece is doing work I can't measure yet."

**Script 13**
"I have held space for clients in the first five minutes of a call when nothing they said made sense yet, because I trusted the process enough to stay curious. I'm going to offer myself the same patience I'd offer them right now."

**Script 14**
"The version of me that published this was doing her best with what she knew today. That's the same standard I hold my clients to. I'm going to hold myself to it too."

**Script 15**
"Silence after publishing is not rejection. It's the reader reading. Some of them are reading right now. I'm going to close the sent folder and go do something else."

---

## STUCK MOMENT 4: The 'I'm Not A Writer' Core Belief
*The thought isn't about this specific piece of copy. It's the deeper conviction that you simply don't have the wiring for this.*

**Script 16**
"Every skill I have as a coach — listening for the thing behind the thing, naming what someone can't quite name for themselves, holding a structure while staying in the feeling — is a writing skill. I already have the raw material. I'm just learning the format."

**Script 17**
"The evidence I'm using to prove I can't write is a small sample from when I didn't know what I know now. I'm not going to let an old data set make my decisions for me. That's not something I'd let a client do."

---

> **How to find your script fast:** Read the stuck-moment heading. Pick the script that makes you exhale slightly. That's the one. Say it, then open the document.

tools.name: The Stuck-Moment Diagnosis Worksheet
tools.instructions: Fill this in before you open the script bank — it takes under two minutes and sends you to exactly the right script instead of reading all seventeen.
tools.content:
# Stuck-Moment Diagnosis Worksheet
*Complete this before you reach for a script. It takes two minutes.*

---

## Step 1 — Name the moment

Check the one that is true right now:

- [ ] I have a blank document open and nothing is coming → **Go to Scripts 1–5**
- [ ] I have words but I've rewritten the same section more than four times → **Go to Scripts 6–10**
- [ ] I've published or sent something and now I regret it → **Go to Scripts 11–15**
- [ ] The problem isn't this piece of copy — it's the belief that I'm not a writer → **Go to Scripts 16–17**

---

## Step 2 — Name the specific fear

Complete this sentence (don't edit it, just write):

*"If I publish this and it doesn't work, it will prove that _____________________________."*

---

## Step 3 — Check the fear against your coaching standard

Answer this question:

*"If a client said this exact sentence to me about their own work, what would I say back to them?"*

Write that response here: _____________________________

---

## Step 4 — Return to the document

Set a timer for **20 minutes**. Write without switching tabs. When the timer ends, you may evaluate. Not before.

---

> **The point of this worksheet:** The fear that surfaces when you write is usually not about the copy. It's about what the copy's performance will mean about you. Naming it specifically — the way you'd name it for a client — is what breaks the loop. Then you go back to work.

tools.name: The Discovery-Call-to-Copy Translation SOP
tools.instructions: Run this SOP once before any copy session where you're stuck on blank-page syndrome — it converts your existing coaching fluency into raw copy material in under fifteen minutes.
tools.content:
# The Discovery-Call-to-Copy Translation SOP
*Use this when: you can't find a starting point for any piece of copy — sales page section, email, invitation.*
*Time required: 12–15 minutes*

---

## Why this works
You already hold a discovery call and have prospects say "you completely get me" within fifteen minutes. That's not a different skill from copywriting — it's the same skill, applied verbally. This SOP transfers what you already do on a call into written form, so you're never starting from nothing.

---

## Step 1 — Pull one real client or prospect from memory (3 minutes)

Think of the last person who booked a call or enrolled after saying something like "that really resonated" or "you just described exactly what's been happening."

Write their first name (or a one-word identifier) here: **[CLIENT NAME/IDENTIFIER]**

Write the single sentence they said that told you they felt understood:
**"[EXACT OR NEAR-EXACT QUOTE FROM THAT PERSON]"**

---

## Step 2 — Reconstruct the moment before they found you (3 minutes)

Answer these three questions in one sentence each. Write fast, don't edit:

1. What had they just tried that hadn't worked, right before they came to you?
**[THEIR LAST FAILED ATTEMPT]**

2. What were they telling themselves about why it hadn't worked?
**[THEIR PRIVATE STORY ABOUT THEMSELVES]**

3. What was the specific moment — the sentence they were mid-way through, the conversation they ran out of answer in — that made them decide they needed outside help?
**[THE SPECIFIC TRIGGER MOMENT]**

---

## Step 3 — Translate to copy (5 minutes)

Now complete this template using only what you wrote in Steps 1 and 2. Do not think about copy. Think about that person.

> *"If you've just [THEIR LAST FAILED ATTEMPT], and you're telling yourself [THEIR PRIVATE STORY ABOUT THEMSELVES] — that's not a talent problem. That's a [WHAT YOUR METHOD REFRAMES IT AS] problem. And [YOUR METHOD NAME] is built to solve exactly that."*

This is the opening of your next piece of copy. It needs no polish yet. It just needs to be true.

---

## Step 4 — Read it against the real person (2 minutes)

Read what you wrote in Step 3 aloud. Ask yourself:

- Would [CLIENT NAME] recognise themselves in this?
- [ ] Yes — keep going from here
- [ ] Not quite — which word is wrong? Change only that word, then keep going

---

> **What you've just done:** You reversed the Client Psychology Reverse-Map into a writing starter. Instead of beginning with a blank page about your offer, you began with a real human being's specific moment — the same place your best discovery calls begin. Every piece of copy you write in this programme starts here.

tools.name: The 48-Hour Reframe Recovery Checklist
tools.instructions: Run this checklist any time you've lost two or more hours to fear-avoidance on a copy task — it resets the session and gets you back to producing in under ten minutes.
tools.content:
# The 48-Hour Reframe Recovery Checklist
*For when you've been avoiding the document for hours (or days) and need a structured re-entry.*

---

## PHASE 1 — Acknowledge the stop (2 minutes)

- [ ] I have named the specific stuck moment (blank page / rewrite loop / post-publish spiral / core belief)
- [ ] I have read the matching script from the Reframe Bank — not all seventeen, just the one for my moment
- [ ] I have not opened social media, my inbox, or any other tab since reading the script

---

## PHASE 2 — Reduce the scope (3 minutes)

- [ ] I have identified the ONE section or ONE email I am writing today — not the whole sales page, not the full sequence
- [ ] I have written the section name at the top of a blank document: **[SECTION NAME, e.g. "Opening paragraph of sales page hero section"]**
- [ ] I have given myself a word limit for this session: **[NUMBER, e.g. 150 words]** — I am writing that and only that

---

## PHASE 3 — Source the raw material (5 minutes)

- [ ] I have completed Steps 1–2 of the Discovery-Call-to-Copy Translation SOP (or I already have the raw material from a previous session)
- [ ] I have the one real client or prospect in mind whose specific moment I am writing toward
- [ ] I have their words — or as close to their words as I can reconstruct — in front of me

---

## PHASE 4 — Produce without evaluating (20 minutes)

- [ ] Timer is set for 20 minutes
- [ ] Script bank tab is open; all other tabs are closed
- [ ] I have written my target word count — or more — before the timer ends
- [ ] I have not deleted anything during this session (mark, highlight, or bracket instead)

---

## PHASE 5 — Close the loop

- [ ] I have saved the document
- [ ] I have noted what I produced: **[WHAT I WROTE TODAY — e.g. "Hero section opening, 140 words, first draft"]**
- [ ] I have set the next session time now, before I close the document: **[DATE / TIME OF NEXT SESSION]**

---

> **The rule this checklist enforces:** Production and evaluation are different cognitive modes. This session was production. Evaluation — where you decide if it's good — is a different session, scheduled separately. What you produced today counts, even if it doesn't feel like it yet.

nextStep.body: Now that you have the scripts to keep fear from stopping you, the next step is the one that changes what your copy actually does. Inside the programme, the Client Psychology Reverse-Map module walks you through identifying the specific trigger moment your best-fit buyer experiences right before they decide they need outside help — and mapping every section of your sales page to that moment instead of to a general description of their pain. Bring your current sales page draft (or the raw output from your first copy session using this toolkit) and run it through the Reverse-Map. That's where the copy stops sounding like a description and starts sounding like a catch.
